summary: Defines how CAPWAP is used with IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs, so a central Access Controller can manage wireless termination points in a standard way. This is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary:
A wireless access point can be managed on its own, or it can be managed by a central controller that tells it what radio settings to use and which users to let in. The protocol for that second arrangement is CAPWAP, and this document says how CAPWAP works with Wi-Fi, that is, with IEEE 802.11.

It covers where each function runs, in the access point or in the controller, how a station is set up when it joins, how it is moved between access points, and how the controller refreshes the keys used to protect broadcast traffic.

subtitle: Defines how the CAPWAP access-point control protocol carries IEEE 802.11 traffic between a wireless access point and its controller.

tldr.problem: The CAPWAP protocol lets a central controller manage wireless access points, but on its own it says nothing about any particular radio technology. A binding specification is needed to say which messages, message elements and radio settings an 802.11 network needs.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines the IEEE 802.11 binding: the wireless binding identifier, the division of work between the access point and the controller in Split MAC and Local MAC mode, new WLAN configuration messages, 802.11-specific message elements for discovery, configuration and statistics, and the rules for carrying 802.11 frames and their quality-of-service markings.
tldr.outcome: A controller can create, update and delete WLANs on an access point, install per-station keys and policies, refresh group keys, and control how packets are prioritised. The binding covers the IEEE 802.11-2007 standard and does not officially support IEEE 802.11n.

today: RFC 5416 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It is the IEEE 802.11 binding for the CAPWAP protocol specified in RFC 5415, and it covers the IEEE 802.11-2007 standard rather than IEEE 802.11n.

sections.title: The CAPWAP Architecture and This Binding
sections.content:
Wireless LAN product architectures have evolved from single autonomous access points to systems consisting of a centralized Access Controller (AC) and Wireless Termination Points (WTPs). The general goal of centralized control architectures is to move access control, including user authentication and authorization, mobility management and radio management, from the single access point to a centralized controller.

The CAPWAP protocol of RFC 5415 defines an extensible protocol that lets an Access Controller manage wireless agnostic Wireless Termination Points. The CAPWAP protocol itself does not include any specific wireless technologies; instead, it relies on a binding specification to extend it to a particular wireless technology. This document is that binding for the IEEE 802.11 Wireless Local Area Network protocol. It defines the use of CAPWAP control message fields, new control messages and message elements, and includes the minimum required definitions for a binding-specific Statistics message element, Station message element and WTP Radio Information message element.

The goals are stated as two points. First, to centralize the authentication and policy enforcement functions for an IEEE 802.11 wireless network, with the AC possibly also providing centralized bridging, forwarding and encryption of user traffic. Second, to enable shifting of higher-level protocol processing from the WTP, leaving the time-critical applications of wireless control and access in the WTP and making efficient use of the computing power available in WTPs that are subject to severe cost pressure.

Two limits are worth noting. The binding supports only the IEEE 802.11-2007 specification, and it does not support the ad hoc network mode of that standard, nor the four-address data frame format commonly referred to as Wireless Bridges. The protocol does not officially support IEEE 802.11n, although a WTP may advertise support for an 802.11n radio, and other IEEE specifications published outside this document, such as IEEE 802.11v and IEEE 802.11r, are not supported through this binding and must be addressed either through a separate CAPWAP binding or an update to this one. Because the Wi-Fi Alliance's WiFi Protect Access and WiFi MultiMedia specifications are widely used in the industry, this binding requires the use of both.

The extensions defined here apply solely to the interface between the WTP and the AC. Communication between controllers, and between stations and the controller, is strictly outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: CAPWAP is the protocol a central controller uses to manage wireless access points. It is written to work with any radio technology, so a binding document is needed to fill in the details for each one. This document is that detail for Wi-Fi.

sections.title: Split MAC and Local MAC
sections.content:
For both the Split and Local MAC approaches, the CAPWAP functions, as defined in the taxonomy of RFC 4118, reside in the Access Controller. To provide system component interoperability, the WTP and AC MUST support 802.11 encryption and decryption at the WTP, and MAY support 802.11 encryption and decryption at the AC.

In a Split MAC architecture, the Distribution and Integration services reside on the AC, so all user data is tunnelled between the WTP and the AC, while all the real-time 802.11 services, including the Beacon and Probe Response frames, are handled on the WTP. The remaining 802.11 MAC management frames are supported on the AC, including the Association Request frame, which allows the AC to be involved in the access policy enforcement portion of the 802.11 protocol. The IEEE 802.1X, EAP and RSNA key management functions are also located on the AC, which implies that the Authentication, Authorization and Accounting client also resides on the AC. Admission control sits on the AC, while the real-time scheduling and queuing functions are on the WTP.

The WTP SHALL include the IEEE 802.11 MAC header contents in all frames transmitted to the AC. When 802.11 encryption and decryption is performed at the WTP, the WTP MUST decrypt the uplink frames, MUST set the Protected Frame field to 0, and MUST make the frame format consistent with that of an unprotected 802.11 frame before transmitting the frames to the AC. The fields added to a protected frame, the Initialization Vector, the Message Integrity Code and the Integrity Check Value, MUST be stripped off before transmission. For downlink frames, the Protected Frame field MUST be set to 0 by the AC, as the frame being sent is unencrypted, and the WTP applies the required protection policy for the WLAN over the air.

When 802.11 encryption and decryption is performed at the AC instead, the WTP SHALL NOT decrypt the uplink frames before transmitting them to the AC, and the AC and WTP populate the MAC header fields between them: the Version, ToDS, FromDS, Type, SubType, Order, address and QoS Control fields and the frame body come from the AC, while Duration, Sequence Control and the FCS come from the WTP. The FCS field is not included in the frames exchanged between the WTP and the AC: the WTP validates and strips it on the way up and adds it on the way down.

In a Local MAC architecture, the integration service exists on the WTP, and the distribution service MAY reside on either the WTP or the AC. When it resides on the AC, station-generated frames are not forwarded to the AC in their native format, but encapsulated as 802.3 frames. While the MAC is terminated on the WTP, it is necessary for the AC to be aware of mobility events, so the WTP MUST forward the IEEE 802.11 Association Request frames to the AC. The AC MAY reply with a failed Association Response frame, and on receipt of a failed Association Response from the AC the WTP MUST send a Disassociation frame to the station. The IEEE 802.1X, EAP and RSNA key management functions still reside in the AC, so the WTP MUST forward all such frames to the AC and the corresponding responses back to the station.

One characteristic applies to both modes. When the WTP tunnels data packets to the AC, and the other way round, the CAPWAP protocol does not guarantee in-order delivery. When the protocol carried over 802.11 is IP, out-of-order delivery is not an issue, because IP has no such requirements, but implementers need to be aware of this before deciding to use CAPWAP.
sections.plainLanguage:
There are two ways to divide the work. In Split MAC the controller does the high-level decisions and all the user traffic is carried back to it, while the access point handles the frames that must be answered immediately. In Local MAC the access point keeps the MAC layer and passes only what it needs to the controller.

The choice matters for encryption. If the access point encrypts, it strips the encryption fields off before sending a frame to the controller, and the controller sends unencrypted frames back for the access point to protect.

sections.title: Roaming Between Access Points
sections.content:
Once a client has successfully associated with the network in a secure fashion, it is likely to attempt to roam to another WTP. The example in the RFC shows a currently associated station moving from its old WTP to a new one, and is valid for multiple security policies, including IEEE 802.1X and WiFi Protected Access or WPA2. In the event that key caching was employed, the 802.1X authentication step would be eliminated. The example represents the case where crypto services are provided by the WTP, so a case where the AC provided that function would differ in the last step.

The sequence has four parts. The client sends an Association Request and receives an Association Response, which the WTP forwards to the AC. The AC then sends a Station Configuration Request to the new WTP, carrying an Add Station message element with the station MAC address, an IEEE 802.11 Add Station message element with the WLAN ID, and an IEEE 802.11 Session Key with the flag field's 'A' bit set. If there is no key cache entry, the client performs 802.1X authentication and the 802.11 four-way key exchange with the WTP. When the WTP provides the crypto services, the AC then sends a further Station Configuration Request containing a Delete Station message element to the old WTP, and another to the new WTP containing the Add Station element, the station session key with its key value, and an IEEE 802.11 Information Element carrying the RSNIE with the pairwise cipher set to CCMP.

Throughout the exchange the client and the controller exchange traffic through the access point, and the access point forwards the management frames it receives.
sections.plainLanguage: When a laptop moves to another access point, the controller has to be told. It tells the old access point to forget the laptop, and tells the new one which key to use for it. If the controller still remembers the key from before, the laptop does not have to authenticate again.

sections.title: Group Key Refresh
sections.content:
Periodically, the Group Key for the Basic Service Set has to be updated. The AC uses an EAPOL-Key frame to update the group key for each station in the BSS. While the AC is updating the group key, each Layer 2 broadcast frame transmitted to the BSS needs to be duplicated and transmitted using both the current group key and the new one. Once the group key update process has completed, broadcast frames transmitted to the BSS will be encrypted using the new group key alone.

Where the work happens depends on the mode. In the case of Split MAC, the AC needs to duplicate all broadcast packets and update the key index so that the packet is transmitted using both the current and the new group key, which ensures that all stations in the BSS receive the broadcast frames. In the case of Local MAC, the WTP needs to duplicate and transmit the broadcast frames using the appropriate index for the same reason.

The procedure itself has four steps. The AC signals the update to the group key using an IEEE 802.11 WLAN Configuration Request message that includes an IEEE 802.11 Update WLAN message element with the new group key, its index, the Transmit Sequence Counter for the group key and the Key Status set to 3, meaning that the group key update is beginning. The AC then begins updating the group key for each station. During this time, the AC for Split MAC, or the WTP for Local MAC, MUST duplicate broadcast packets and transmit them encrypted with both the current and the new group key. When the AC has completed the update to all stations in the BSS, it MUST transmit another IEEE 802.11 WLAN Configuration Request message including an IEEE 802.11 Update WLAN message element that contains the new group key, its index, and the Key Status set to 4, meaning the group key update is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: The key that protects broadcast traffic has to be replaced from time to time. While the new key is being installed at each device, every broadcast frame has to be sent twice, once with the old key and once with the new one, so that no device misses a broadcast. Once every device has the new key, the duplicate copies stop.

sections.title: Quality of Service Tagging
sections.content:
When a WLAN is created on the WTP, a default Quality of Service policy is established through the IEEE 802.11 WTP Quality of Service message element. That default policy causes the WTP to use the default QoS values for any station associated with the WLAN. The AC MAY also override the policy for a given station by sending the IEEE 802.11 Update Station QoS message element, known as a station-specific QoS policy. Beyond those, the 802.11 protocol lets a station request special QoS treatment for a specific flow through the Traffic Specification information elements found in the QoS Action Frame, or through the Wi-Fi Alliance's WMM specification. This requires the WTP to observe the Status Code in the Add Traffic System responses from the AC and provide the services requested, and to observe the Reason Code information element in the Delete Traffic System responses in order to remove the policy associated with a Traffic Specification.

The Tagging Policy field of the IEEE 802.11 WTP Quality of Service element indicates how packets are to be tagged. It has five bits, two of which indicate the type of QoS to be used by the WTP. The 'P' bit tells the WTP to use the 802.1p mechanism, and the 'Q' bit then tells it which 802.1p priority values to use. The 'D' bit tells the WTP to use the Differentiated Services Code Point mechanism, and the 'I' and 'O' bits tell it which values to use in the inner header, the station's original packet, or the outer header, the latter of which is only valid when tunnelling is enabled.

With 802.1p, the WTP adds an 802.1Q header with the priority field set according to the policy, and this tagging is only valid for interfaces that support 802.1p. When the 'Q' bit is set to 1 the WTP marks the priority field in the 802.1Q header with either the default or the station-specific 802.1p policy. When it is 0, the WTP marks it with the value found in the User Priority field of the QoS Control field of the 802.11 header, falling back to the 'Q=1' behaviour if that field is absent.

With DSCP, the WTP marks the DSCP field of both the IPv4 and IPv6 headers. The 'I' bit controls the inner packet and the 'O' bit the outer packet. Where tunnelling is not used, both 'O=1' and 'O=0' are invalid for station data frames; 'I=1' sets the DSCP field of the station's packet to the default policy or the station-specific policy if one exists, and 'I=0' means the WTP MUST NOT modify the DSCP field of the station's packet. Where tunnelling is used, 'O=1' sets the DSCP field in the tunnel header to the policy value and 'O=0' sets it to the value found in the inner packet's DSCP field; if encryption services are provided by the AC the packet is encrypted, so the WTP cannot reach the inner DSCP field and uses the behaviour of the 'O' bit set, which also happens when the inner packet is neither IPv4 nor IPv6 and so has no DSCP field. The 'I' bit behaves the same way for the inner packet. The use of the DSCP and 802.1p mechanisms is not mutually exclusive: an AC MAY request that a WTP use none, one, or both at the same time.

Management frames get their own recommendation. All IEEE 802.11 MAC management frames SHOULD use the 802.1p precedence value of 7, except for Probe Requests, which SHOULD use 4, and they SHOULD use the CS6 per-hop behaviour for DSCP, while Probe Requests should use the Low Drop Assured Forwarding per-hop behaviour.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller can tell the access point how to mark packets so that the network treats voice or video differently from ordinary traffic. It can do that with the priority field used on wired networks, with the traffic class field used in IP headers, or with both. It can also set a default for the whole wireless network and a different one for a single device.

sections.title: New Control Messages and Message Elements
sections.content:
This document defines two CAPWAP control messages that are specific to the IEEE 802.11 binding: the IEEE 802.11 WLAN Configuration Request and the IEEE 802.11 WLAN Configuration Response. The IANA Enterprise number used with these messages is 13277, and the resulting message type values are 3398913 for the request and 3398914 for the response. The CAPWAP header also requires a Wireless Binding Identifier, and this document uses the value one.

The WLAN Configuration Request is sent by the AC to the WTP to change the services the WTP provides, and is used to create, update or delete a WLAN on the WTP. It is sent either as a result of a manual administrative process, such as deleting a WLAN, or automatically to create a WLAN, in which case it is sent after the CAPWAP Configuration Update Response of RFC 5415 has been received by the AC. On receiving the message, the WTP modifies the necessary services and transmits a WLAN Configuration Response. That response acknowledges receipt of the request and indicates that the requested configuration was applied successfully, or that an error occurred on the WTP.

A WTP MAY provide service for more than one WLAN, so every WLAN is identified through a numerical index. A WTP capable of supporting up to 16 SSIDs could accept up to 16 WLAN Configuration Request messages that include the Add WLAN message element. Since the index is the primary identifier for a WLAN, an AC MAY attempt to ensure that the same WLAN is identified through the same index number on all of its WTPs; an AC that does not follow that approach MUST find some other means of maintaining a WLAN-Identifier-to-SSID mapping table.

Only one of the IEEE 802.11 Add WLAN, Delete WLAN or Update WLAN message elements MUST be present in the request. An IEEE 802.11 Information Element or a Vendor-Specific Payload MAY also be present. The response MUST include a Result Code, and MAY include the IEEE 802.11 Assigned WTP BSSID element or a Vendor-Specific Payload.

The binding also says how BSSIDs are assigned. The binding enables the WTP to assign BSSIDs upon creation of a WLAN, and although manufacturers are free to assign them using any arbitrary mechanism, it is advised that where possible the BSSIDs are assigned as a contiguous block. One possible method is to assign the address using the base BSSID address plus the WLAN ID. The WTP communicates the maximum number of BSSIDs that it supports during configuration, through the IEEE 802.11 WTP WLAN Radio Configuration message element.

Several of the standard CAPWAP control messages carry 802.11-specific message elements. The Discovery Request and Response, Primary Discovery Request and Response, and Join Request and Response messages MUST each include an IEEE 802.11 WTP Radio Information element, and that element MUST be present for every radio in the WTP. The Configuration Status Request and Response messages and the Configuration Update Request message MAY carry elements such as the Antenna, Direct Sequence Control, MAC Operation, Multi-Domain Capability, OFDM Control, Supported Rates, Rate Set, Tx Power, Tx Power Level, WTP Quality of Service and WTP Radio Configuration elements. The Station Configuration Request MAY carry the Station, Station Session Key, Station QoS Profile and Update Station QoS elements, and the WTP Event Request MAY carry the MIC Countermeasures, RSNA Error Report from Station and Statistics elements.
sections.plainLanguage: The binding adds two new control messages for creating and deleting wireless networks on an access point, and says which pieces of radio and station information go into the existing CAPWAP messages. Each radio and each wireless network also gets a number, so the controller can refer to them.

sections.title: How 802.11 Frames Are Carried
sections.content:
The CAPWAP protocol defines the CAPWAP data message, which is used to encapsulate a wireless payload. For IEEE 802.11, the 802.11 header and payload are encapsulated, excluding the 802.11 FCS checksum, and the checksum is handled by the WTP. This lets the WTP validate an 802.11 frame before sending it to the AC. Similarly, when the AC wishes to transmit a frame to a station, the WTP computes and adds the FCS checksum.

An optional CAPWAP header field, the Wireless Specific Information, is used only with CAPWAP data messages, and its format depends on the direction of the message. For messages from the WTP to the AC the field carries the IEEE 802.11 Frame Info, which holds radio and PHY-specific information associated with the frame. For messages sent by the AC to the WTP the format used is that of the Destination WLANs field. In both cases the two optional headers fit in the Data field of the Wireless Specific Information header.

The IEEE 802.11 Frame Info field has three parts. RSSI, the Received Signal Strength Indication, is a signed 8-bit value giving the received signal strength in dBm. SNR, the signal-to-noise ratio of the received frame, is a signed 8-bit value in dB. The Data Rate is a 16-bit unsigned value expressing the data rate of the packets received by the WTP in units of 0.1 Mbps: a packet received at 5.5 Mbps is set to 55, while 11 Mbps is set to 110.
sections.plainLanguage: User traffic from a wireless device is carried to the controller inside a CAPWAP data message. Alongside it, the access point reports how strong the signal was, how noisy the radio link was, and at what rate the frame arrived, all in a few bytes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A complete threat analysis of the CAPWAP protocol can be found in RFC 5418. This section covers the security of IEEE 802.11 itself when used with CAPWAP.

When used with an IEEE 802.11 infrastructure with WEP encryption, the CAPWAP protocol does not add any new vulnerabilities. Derived session keys between the station and the WTP can be compromised, resulting in many well-documented attacks, so implementers SHOULD discourage the use of WEP and encourage the use of technically sound cryptographic solutions such as those in an IEEE 802.11 RSN. Station authentication is performed using IEEE 802.1X, and consequently EAP, and implementers SHOULD use EAP methods meeting the requirements specified in RFC 4017.

When used with IEEE 802.11 RSN security, the CAPWAP protocol may introduce new vulnerabilities, depending on whether the link security, that is packet encryption and integrity verification, is provided by the WTP or the AC. When the link security function is provided by the AC, no new security concerns are introduced.

When the WTP provides link security, a new vulnerability exists when the client is not the first to associate to the WTP or ESSID, so that other clients are associated and a group key already exists, and traffic has been broadcast under the existing group key. Under these circumstances the receive sequence counter associated with the group key is non-zero, but because the AC anchors the four-way handshake with the client, the exact value of the counter is not known when the AC constructs the message containing the group key. The client will update its counter to the current valid value on receipt of a valid multicast or broadcast message, but prior to that, previous multicast or broadcast traffic secured with the existing group key may be replayed and the client will accept it as valid.

Typically, busy networks produce numerous multicast or broadcast frames per second, so the window of opportunity for such a replay is expected to be very small, and in most conditions it is expected that replayed frames could be detected and logged by the WTP. The only way to close the window completely is to provide the exact counter value in message 3 of the four-way handshake, and any other approach simply narrows it to varying degrees. Given the low relative threat level, the additional complexity is not warranted, and this specification provides for a calculated risk in this regard. The AC SHOULD use a receive sequence counter of 0 when computing message 3 of the four-way 802.11i handshake, unless it has knowledge of a more optimal value.
sections.plainLanguage: With old-style WEP encryption the protocol adds no new risk, but WEP itself is broken and should not be used. With the modern RSN security there is one narrow weakness when the access point, rather than the controller, does the encrypting: a broadcast frame sent just before a new device joins could be replayed to that device. The window for that is very short, and the RFC accepts the risk rather than adding complexity.

messages.label: BEACON
messages.note: Generated by the WTP from the IEEE 802.11 Add WLAN element.

messages.label: PROBE REQUEST
messages.note: Forwarded to the AC for optional processing.

messages.label: 802.11 AUTH AND ASSOCIATION
messages.note: The WTP forwards these to the AC, which responds to the client.

messages.label: STATION CONFIGURATION REQUEST
messages.note: Carries Add Station, IEEE 802.11 Add Station and IEEE 802.11 Session Key with flag A.

messages.label: STATION CONFIGURATION REQUEST
messages.note: Carries the pairwise session key and the RSNIE.

messages.label: 802.11 DATA
messages.note: All station data frames are tunnelled between the WTP and the AC.

fields.name: RSSI
fields.desc: Received signal strength in dBm; a signed 8-bit value.

fields.name: SNR
fields.desc: Signal-to-noise ratio of the received frame in dB; a signed 8-bit value.

fields.name: Data Rate
fields.desc: Data rate in units of 0.1 Mbps; 5.5 Mbps is set to 55 and 11 Mbps to 110.
